text: Idempotent sounds academic, but it describes something very practical. A script is idempotent if running it once, or running it five times in a row, leaves the infrastructure in exactly the same end state either way — no duplicate resources, no errors from something that already exists. The goal isn't running it exactly once, it's trusting that any number of runs converges on the same correct result.

Scripts get rerun far more often than people expect: a deployment pipeline retries a failed step, a teammate reruns last week's setup script against a new environment, or you rerun your own script after fixing one line, not realizing it already created half the resources on the first attempt. If the script isn't idempotent, any of those situations can leave duplicate resources or infrastructure in a state nobody intended.

Here's the problem in practice. New-AzResourceGroup -Name rg-prod -Location eastus succeeds the first time it runs. Run that exact same line again — because the pipeline retried, or because you reran the script — and it throws an error, because rg-prod already exists.

The fix is to check first, and only act if the check says you need to. Get-AzResourceGroup with -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue checks whether rg-prod already exists, without throwing an error if it doesn't. If it's missing, the script creates it. If it's already there, the script does nothing and moves on — no error, no duplicate, no change in outcome whether this is the first run or the fifth.

That check-then-act shape is the core of idempotent scripting, and it applies far beyond resource groups. Before creating a storage account, check if one with that name already exists. Before adding a tag, check if it's already set to the value you want. Before creating a user account, check if it's already there. The specific cmdlet changes every time; the pattern doesn't.
Up next: error handling in automation scripts, and why a script should fail loudly and stop rather than let a later step run against a half-configured resource.
